title: Piezo-Kerr effect in altermagnets and noncollinear antiferromagnets
authors: Yuqi Liu, Qiu-Shi Huang, Xinfeng Chen, Yilin Han, Run-Wu Zhang, Zhi-Ming Yu, Yugui Yao
abstract: Symmetry is usually viewed as a constraint on physical responses, but it can also be used to design the fields that control them. Here, we adopt the representation-matching principle used to identify conjugate fields of order parameters and apply it to response tensors. A linear coupling, the key ingredient for sign-switching control, is symmetry-allowed when a component (or a combination of components) of the control field and the selected response component share the same irreducible representation of the magnetic point group (MPG) of the system. Applied to the magneto-optical Kerr effect, this principle yields a piezo-Kerr effect, in which specific strain combinations activate a Kerr response forbidden in the unstrained state. Enumerating all 122 MPGs, we identify 16 groups in which the unstrained Kerr response is forbidden while a linear strain-induced contribution is allowed. These groups are realized by altermagnets and noncollinear antiferromagnets with symmetry-enforced vanishing net magnetization. The active strain channels and the associated first-order sign reversals follow directly from symmetry. First-principles calculations for bulk MnTe$_{2}$ and CoF$_{2}$, and Cr$_{2}$Se$_{2}$O and Cr$_{2}$Te$_{2}$O monolayers confirm these predictions. In these materials, the Kerr rotation vanishes without strain, whereas 0.5-3% strain produces rotations ranging from tens to hundreds of millidegrees, and reversing the matched strain channel reverses the Kerr sign. These results establish a general route to large and switchable Kerr responses emerging from symmetry-forbidden states in compensated magnets.
summary: This work develops a general theoretical framework using group theory to predict the piezo-Kerr effect in antiferromagnets. By matching the symmetry representations of strain and the Kerr response, the authors identify materials where strain can activate a previously forbidden optical response. Calculations confirm that moderate strain induces large, switchable Kerr rotations, offering a robust method for controlling magnetism optically.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish a general, symmetry-based route to achieve large and switchable magneto-optical Kerr responses in compensated magnets (altermagnets and noncollinear antiferromagnets) by activating responses forbidden in the unstrained state.
main_result: They identified 16 magnetic point groups where strain can induce a measurable Kerr effect, and first-principles calculations on materials like MnTe2 and Cr2Te2O confirm large, sign-reversing Kerr rotations upon applying moderate strain.
method: The study employs the 'representation-matching principle' from group theory to determine symmetry-allowed linear couplings between strain components and the Kerr response tensor, validated by first-principles DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The focus is on altermagnets and noncollinear antiferromagnets exhibiting symmetry-enforced vanishing net magnetization. The analysis uses the magnetic point group symmetry to constrain the coupling $	heta_i \propto \sum \Lambda_{i,jk} \epsilon_{jk}$.
key_observables: Kerr rotation ($	heta_z$), spin splitting, and the strain-induced change in $	heta_z$ (reaching tens to hundreds of millidegrees).
important_parameters: Strain magnitude (0.5–3%), photon energy ($\hbar\omega$), and the irreducible representations (IRRs) of the Magnetic Point Group (MPG).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the linear coupling approximation ($	heta_i \propto \epsilon_{jk}$) and the symmetry constraints derived from the MPG.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structures, band structures (showing spin splitting under strain), and the calculated dependence of the Kerr rotation ($	heta_z$) on applied uniaxial strain for various materials.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by establishing the theoretical framework using representation theory to identify symmetry-allowed couplings, enumerating the relevant magnetic point groups, and then applying these principles via first-principles DFT calculations to predict and confirm the large, switchable piezo-Kerr effect in specific material classes.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum information, the detailed symmetry analysis and the ability to engineer a measurable optical response (Kerr effect) using mechanical strain provides a powerful, symmetry-dictated control mechanism relevant to spintronics and magnetoelectric coupling in quantum materials.
